prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change

A Payment inside the `RawTransactions` of a Batch now follows the `DeliverMax` rule on output and input, like a top-level Payment. `simulate` and `submit` with `tx_blob` follow it too.

- `insertDeliverMax` applies the rule to each inner Payment of a Batch, so every method that already calls it renders inner Payments with `DeliverMax`. `simulate` and `submit` with `tx_blob` now call it on the `tx_json` they return.
- `removeDeliverMax` replaces the alias handling in `checkPayment`, maps `DeliverMax` to `Amount` in inner Payments as well, and runs before `checkFee` (and before `autofillTx` in `simulate`).

Fixes #8557

## Context of Change

`insertDeliverMax` only acted on a top-level `ttPAYMENT`, and `checkPayment` only aliased a top-level Payment. `DeliverMax` is not an `SField`, so `STParsedJSON` rejected it in an inner Payment as an unknown field. While tracing the callers I found that `simulate` had no `DeliverMax` handling at all, and `doSubmit` rendered `tx_json` without calling `insertDeliverMax`.

The alias is resolved before `checkFee` because `getTxFee` parses `tx_json` to compute the fee. A Batch fee depends on its inner transactions, so an unresolved inner `DeliverMax` fails that parse and the autofilled fee falls back to the reference fee. `autofillTx` in `simulate` has the same dependency for a multi-signed Payment.

## API Impact

- [ ] Public API: New feature (new methods and/or new fields)
- [x] Public API: Breaking change (in general, breaking changes should only impact the next api_version)
- [ ] `libxrpl` change (any change that may affect `libxrpl` or dependents of `libxrpl`)
- [ ] Peer protocol change (must be backward compatible or bump the peer protocol version)

In API version 2, inner Payments and the `tx_json` returned by `simulate` and by `submit` with `tx_blob` now carry only `DeliverMax`, not `Amount`, matching every other Payment in v2. API version 1 gains `DeliverMax` next to `Amount`. `DeliverMax` is now accepted where it was rejected. Entries are in `API-CHANGELOG.md`.

- What happens when we want to write faster than NuDB is able to write? We have to do something to slow down the write rate.
- Could we just slow down the writes since there is no rush?
- Yes, but we don't want to block all threads writing to NuDB. We could add a priority and make online_delete low priority. (That is the only thing that really generates surges of writes; also consider: fetching ledger history; closing a new ledger is a very small surge)
  - If buffer is somewhat full, pause the low priority writes.
  - Need to expose the "progress" of online_delete since it will take more time.
- Need to bound memory use so it's not infinite. Current approach allows writes to grow at a certain rate and if writes exceed the rate, we slow down all code that tries to write. It would slow down online_delete which is something we should do; but that would also slow down high-priority code which is advancing the ledger.
- NuDB tracks its own bytes/sec or objects/sec write rate and can tell if writes are coming in faster than that. It can measure what % of the server's capacity is being used. What should we do with that information? We can slow something down, but what?

comments.author: intelliot
comments.body:
https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/pull/4503 writes asynchronously to nudb with a background thread, but it has an upper limit of records that can be in the queue to be written. When reached, writes are blocked. Online deletion copies a ledger and ensures that it writes the entire ledger to nudb. This amount of data being written likely causes further writes to be blocked until the data is written. This includes persisting new records for each new ledger produced, which is synchronous for consensus. This causes desyncs. This PR (#4762) is expected to fix this.

If #4882 (which just reverts #4503) is merged, then #4503+#4762 (combined) can still be considered for testing+merging in the future.

We can design micro-benchmarks to show how it affects NuDB itself. Write prioritization is too much complexity, but if NuDB could write faster, then that was the whole point of #4503.

prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change
Removes a limit that blocks nodestore writes. This delays consensus because each new ledger is persisted during consensus processing.



### Context of Change
This removes the check that limits write batch size and blocks when the limit is reached. It also adds logging to indicate when the limit is exceeded. The trade-off is that the pending writes consume memory until they are persisted, so memory can increase without the limit. But since blocking writes result in consensus instability, the existing behavior is a proactive pessimization. Ultimately, pending writes either increase due to increased input (transaction volume), or because of I/O slowdown. If the IO and memory subsystem can't handle the throughput then the process will be unstable regardless.

prs.body:
Add new transaction submission API field, "sync_mode", which determines behavior of the server while submitting transactions: 1) sync (default): Process transactions in a batch immediately,
   and return only once the transaction has been processed.
2) async: Put transaction into the batch for the next processing
   interval and return immediately.
3) wait: Put transaction into the batch for the next processing
   interval and return only after it is processed.

This PR is related to 2 others that, when combined, increase throughput significantly:
https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/pull/4503
https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/pull/4505



## High Level Overview of Change
This improves transaction throughput. For background, transactions are applied to the open ledger in batches. Only one batch is applied at a time. As they are received from either a client or a peer, transactions are added to a batch. If no batches are being processed, then the current batch is processed immediately. Otherwise, it will be processed once the current batch completes. Batches are applied continuously until no more transactions are queued this way. This pattern optimizes both throughput and latency, but only if applying batches does not contend with other activities.

However, the problem is that batch application contends with numerous other activities for the MasterLock and the LedgerMaster lock. As transaction volume increases, so does lock contention. Analysis under heavy transaction load shows that a large amount of time is spent in each transaction batch setting up the open ledger for modification. However, each individual transaction takes a very small amount of time. More importantly, duration preparing to modify the ledger is not affected by the size of the batch! Instead, this duration is related to the amount of transactions in the current open ledger--as transaction volume increases, so does the time it takes to apply each batch.

For example, assume it takes 5ms to prepare the ledger for each batch, and 50us per transaction. Minimizing wall clock time, and therefore lock contention, means minimizing the number of batches. To put in perspective, single transactions submitted just under 5ms apart would consume all available wall clock time, with the vast majority simply preparing the open ledger for modification! That's not a problem if our only workload is applying transactions. But other things need to use the lock, also.

The solution implemented instead attempts to apply batches approximately every 100ms, or 10 times per second. To contrast with the above example, reducing the number of batches this way would reduce open ledger preparation time from nearly 1 full second to only 50ms, while actual transaction processing is a trivial 10ms. That's a 94% reduction in lock contention! That's a contrived example, of course, but it plays out in testing--as transaction volume increases, lock contention decreases and the server is able to process significantly higher volume.

Along with this fix is an enhancement to the submission API. Namely, the existing behavior is to immediately process transactions as they are submitted by the client (but not the peer). However, this tends to diminish the effectiveness of the fix as volume submitted directly to the server increases. This is because more batches are being applied. The problem exhibits itself only under very high volume, but if not addressed will cause problems as livenet volume increases. The API enhancement creates an optional new field called "sync_mode" with the following possible settings:
    1) sync (default): Process transactions in a batch immediately,
       and return only once the transaction has been processed.
    2) async: Put transaction into the batch for the next processing
       interval and return immediately. If successful, return a new code: terSUBMITTED.
    3) wait: Put transaction into the batch for the next processing
       interval and return only after it is processed.

Trade-offs for each option are as follows:
* sync: This is identical to existing behavior, so no users will be suprised by this as long as this stays the default. However, it will lead to instability of the server as described above.
* async: This returns immediately, and is actually faster for the client. However, transaction submission errors that occur only once the transaction is applied will be unknown to the client. This should be used for performance testing.
* wait: This is the slowest for the client, but it allows the server to keep up with the network as if the transaction had been submitted "async".

## High Level Overview of Change

Remove the per-insertion heap allocations from `Batch::preflight`. The duplicate-inner-transaction and duplicate-sequence/ticket checks used an `std::unordered_set` and an `std::unordered_map` of `std::unordered_set`s; they are now `std::flat_set`s backed by a `boost::container::small_vector` sized to `kMaxBatchTxCount`, so neither container ever leaves inline storage.

## Context of Change

`Batch::preflight` runs for every submitted and relayed Batch, including those about to be rejected, and the two containers it used allocate per node (and, for the map, per distinct account) to hold at most eight entries. The map of sets is flattened to a set of `(account, sequence-or-ticket)` pairs: pair membership was the only query, and the preceding `temSEQ_AND_TICKET` checks already guarantee exactly one of `Sequence` and `TicketSequence` is set, so the two insert sites collapse into one. Sequences and tickets keep sharing one key space per account, and the checks run at the same point in the per-inner loop, so every result code is unchanged. No amendment is needed.

## API Impact

- [ ] Public API: New feature (new methods and/or new fields)
- [ ] Public API: Breaking change (in general, breaking changes should only impact the next api_version)
- [x] `libxrpl` change (any change that may affect `libxrpl` or dependents of `libxrpl`)
- [ ] Peer protocol change (must be backward compatible or bump the peer protocol version)

The change is internal to `Batch::preflight`; no `libxrpl` interface changes.

## Before / After

1. Improvement to existing functionality.
2. Memory allocation behavior of `Batch::preflight`; transaction results are unchanged.
3. Preflight of Batch transactions on the submit and relay paths (`checkValidity`, `TxQ::apply`, ledger building).

🟠 **Severity: HIGH**

The outer batch is added to `byFee_`/`byAccount_` inside `applyImpl()` (which releases the mutex on return), then inner txs are added via `processInnerBatch()` under separate lock acquisitions. If `accept()` runs between, it can process and erase the outer batch before inner txs are added, leaving orphaned inner txs permanently blocking account sequence slots in `byAccount_`.
Helpful? Add 👍 / 👎

<details>
<summary>💡 Fix Suggestion</summary>

**Suggestion:** The race condition occurs because `applyImpl()` acquires the mutex internally at line 1767 and releases it when it returns, leaving a window between the outer batch being added and `processInnerBatch()` adding inner transactions. During this window, `accept()` can erase the outer batch, leaving orphaned inner transactions.

To fix this, ensure atomicity between adding the outer batch and all its inner transactions. Possible approaches:

1. **Restructure to hold the lock across both operations**: Refactor `applyImpl()` to optionally return without releasing the mutex (e.g., via a unique_lock that can be moved out) and pass that lock to `processInnerBatch()`, which would use it instead of acquiring its own lock for each inner tx.

2. **Move inner batch processing inside the lock**: Call `processInnerBatch()` from within `applyImpl()` after `addTxToQueue()` (around line 1880) while still holding the mutex. This requires `processInnerBatch()` to be refactored so inner `applyImpl()` calls don't try to re-acquire the mutex (use a recursive mutex, or split the locked/unlocked portions).

3. **Use a 'pending' state flag**: Add a flag to the batch's queue entry that marks it as 'pending inner txs'. Modify `accept()` to skip entries with this flag. Clear the flag after `processInnerBatch()` completes (under the lock).

Option 2 is likely the cleanest: change `txq_.mutex_` to `std::recursive_mutex`, acquire it in `apply()` before calling `applyImpl()`, and hold it through `processInnerBatch()`. All internal `std::scoped_lock` calls would be no-ops due to recursion.

</details>

reviewCommentsList.body: The constructor reads `tx_->at(sfAccount)` before running `preflight`. For a malformed transaction with no Account field, `at` throws instead of allowing preflight to return its normal malformed/bad-account TER, so `TxQ::apply` can escape with an exception rather than reject the transaction.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: Inner processors are constructed before `TxQ::apply` acquires `txq_.mutex_`, but this initializer reads the non-atomic `FeeMetrics` fields through `getSnapshot()`, while `FeeMetrics::update` mutates those fields under the same mutex. This is a data race during concurrent submissions and ledger processing, and `applyImpl()` overwrites the snapshot under the lock anyway. Remove this eager snapshot and initialize it only in `applyImpl()`.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: These inners are queued as independent candidates, and `accept` later applies them one at a time without consulting the outer batch flags. That loses `tfAllOrNothing`, `tfOnlyOne`, and `tfUntilFailure` semantics: for example, a later inner can apply after an earlier inner fails, or multiple inners can apply for `tfOnlyOne`. Batch execution must remain mode-aware/atomic when dequeued.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: This cached `PreflightResult` is built with a standalone `PreflightContext`, so it has no `parentBatchId` and does not carry `TapBatch`. When the queued inner is later preclaimed, `checkSign` treats it as an ordinary transaction and the unsigned inner can be rejected; a rules/flags refresh also re-preflights it as standalone. Preserve the parent batch ID and batch apply flags in the cached result and in the queued entry.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: The Batch branch computes whether the outer entry is first in its account, but then ignores `isFirst` and checks only the inner accounts. If an inner account becomes eligible while a foreign transaction still precedes the outer Batch, `eraseAndAdvance` can schedule that blocked Batch, consuming retries and potentially dropping it.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: `isFirstInAccount` is only consulted from `eraseAndAdvance`, so the first candidate visited by `accept` is still checked only against the outer account at lines 2087-2099. A high-fee Batch whose outer account is unblocked can therefore be moved to the open ledger while an inner account is still preceded by a foreign queued transaction; when the closed-ledger Batch processing reaches that inner, `tfAllOrNothing` can discard the inners after the outer has already been applied. Apply the Batch-wide readiness check before accepting the initial candidate as well (while preserving the existing ticket ordering rules).

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: On a successful queued Batch, `MaybeTx::apply` only calls `doApply`; `Batch::doApply` returns `tesSUCCESS` without executing its inner transactions (the normal inner loop is in `applyTransaction`). Removing all inner entries here therefore discards them before any queue pass can run them, so a queued Batch advances only the outer sequence and loses the inner effects. Keep/process the inner entries as part of the Batch application instead of deleting them on outer success.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: Queue-full admission can evict an unrelated `byFee_` entry before `processInnerBatch()` has admitted all inners. If a later inner fails, this cleanup removes only the new batch and its inners; it does not restore the evicted transaction (or an evicted batch's inners). A `temINVALID_INNER_BATCH` result can therefore permanently discard unrelated queued work. Admission/eviction needs transactional rollback or all inner constraints must be checked before any eviction.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: This returns every result from `tryClearAccountQueueUpThruTx`, but that helper deliberately returns `{telINSUF_FEE_P, false}` when it cannot clear the prefix (including when it encounters a Batch inner) so the caller can fall back to normal queue admission. Returning it here rejects the candidate instead of reaching `canBeHeld()` and `addTxToQueue()`; the new Trigger 022 scenario will therefore return `telINSUF_FEE_P` rather than queueing. Only return when the result is applied.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: Batch inners are deliberately not inserted into `byFee_`, but they still run `processQueueIsFull()` here. After the outer fills `byFee_` to `maxSize_`, the first fee-free inner has level 0 and cannot beat the positive end-account average, so it returns `telCAN_NOT_QUEUE_FULL` and the whole batch is rolled back. The inner path needs to bypass the global `byFee_` capacity check while retaining per-account admission checks.

issues.title: Support Batch (XLS-56) transactions in simulate (XLS-69) (Version: 3.4.1)
issues.author: yuval99g
issues.body:
## Summary

`simulate` currently rejects `Batch` transactions with `notImpl`. As Batch (BatchV1_1) becomes usable on mainnet, there is no way for wallets, signing UIs or other tooling to preview what a Batch will do before it is signed. This issue proposes extending `simulate` to support Batch.

## Motivation

`simulate` is the main way XRPL clients can show users what a transaction will actually do before they sign it: balance changes, created or deleted objects, and the final result. Batch is the transaction type where that preview matters most:

- **One signature authorizes up to 8 actions.** A user signing a Batch is approving every inner transaction at once, possibly including transactions from other accounts. Without simulation, the signing UI can only show the raw inner transactions, not their combined effect.
- **The combined effect differs from each part.** Inner transactions run in sequence against shared state, so the result of the whole batch can't be read from any single inner transaction.
- **Blind signing is a known attack vector.** Bundling a legitimate-looking action with a harmful one (an unexpected payment, a trust line, an offer) is easier to hide in a Batch than in a single transaction. A dry run is the most reliable way to surface it.
- **Atomic-swap and multi-party flows rely on it.** These are the main motivating use cases for Batch, and participants need to verify what they receive before adding their `BatchSigners` signature.

Without `simulate` support, every wallet and tool has to build its own approximation, and those approximations are inconsistent and often wrong (see Paths Not Taken).

### Current behavior

- `simulate` with a `Batch` returns `notImpl` (blocked in `Simulate.cpp` since #5060).
- The Batch concept docs note that `simulate` only dry-runs a single transaction and can't model adding inner transactions to the consensus set.
- The underlying reason: the outer Batch is applied to the open ledger, while inner transactions are only applied in `applyTransaction` during the ledger build. A dry run on the open ledger would show only the outer layer (fee and sequence), which would be misleading.

## Solution

Allow `simulate` to accept an unsigned `Batch` (with empty `TxnSignature` and empty `BatchSigners` signatures, consistent with how simulate treats signing fields today) and:

1. Apply the outer transaction and its inner transactions in a sandboxed view on top of the current open ledger, using the same `applyBatchTransactions` logic the ledger build uses, and never commit it.
2. Respect the batch mode flag.
3. Return the outer result plus an ordered result for each inner transaction, for example:

```json
{
  "applied": false,
  "engine_result": "tesSUCCESS",
  "tx_json": { "TransactionType": "Batch", "...": "..." },
  "meta": { "...": "outer metadata" },
  "inner_results": [
    {
      "hash": "...",
      "engine_result": "tesSUCCESS",
      "applied": true,
      "tx_json": { "...": "..." },
      "meta": { "ParentBatchID": "...", "AffectedNodes": ["..."] }
    },
    {
      "hash": "...",
      "engine_result": "tecUNFUNDED_PAYMENT",
      "applied": false
    }
  ]
}
```

This mirrors what ends up in a closed ledger (outer, then inners linked by `ParentBatchID`) and would line up with the per-inner outcomes that BatchV2's `BatchResult` (#8532) records. It would also give developers a way to see inner failure results without the debug stream (see #5882).

### Open questions

- Is the `notImpl` a permanent scope decision, or would a PR along these lines be considered?
- Is a sandboxed apply on the open ledger the right approach, or is there a better way to reuse the ledger-build path?
- Autofill: should `simulate` autofill inner `Sequence` values (respecting tickets) the way client libraries do, or require them to be set?

## Paths Not Taken

The obvious client-side workaround is to strip `tfInnerBatchTxn` from each inner transaction and simulate them individually. This gives incorrect results:

1. **No shared state.** Each simulation runs against the current ledger, so inner #2 doesn't see inner #1's effects. Chained flows such as a swap followed by a payment of the proceeds, or funding a new account and then transacting from it, fail or produce wrong results.
2. **Batch modes aren't modeled.** Whether the batch succeeds depends on `tfAllOrNothing` / `tfOnlyOne` / `tfUntilFailure` / `tfIndependent`, which clients would have to reimplement.
3. **Authorization differs.** Inner transactions are authorized through the outer signature and `BatchSigners`, not their own signing fields, so standalone simulations don't reflect the real checks.
4. **Inner transactions can't be sent as-is.** Sending them with `tfInnerBatchTxn` is unsupported, and this path was the source of an assertion crash fixed in BatchV1_1.

## Additional context

- Batch PR: #5060 (adds the `Simulate.cpp` block)
- Related: #5882 (inner Batch failures only visible in the debug stream), #7210 (Batch check ordering in simulate)
- XLS-69 discussion: XRPLF/XRPL-Standards#199
- XLS-56 discussion: XRPLF/XRPL-Standards#162
